I'm skeptical for a large array of reasons.

  1. Refusal to allow open and free research. The US has allowed GMO patent owners to prohibit publication of research related to their organisms without an endorsement from the company in question, and they've taken the government up on this "right." Monsanto, as the typical example, specifically prohibits and allows certain areas of research and ultimately all research must be rubber stamped from them before being published. Fortunately the first Monsanto seeds have very recently come out of patent protection and so we should be seeing free research published in the coming years.

  2. Misleading marketing. GMOs are routinely advertised by advocates as being akin to how we've long since cross bred plants and animals to favor certain traits. That's misleading and inaccurate. GMOs are more akin to the mythological chimera - a monster with the head of a lion, body of a goat and tail of a snake. GMOs combine traits from completely unrelated organisms and mash them together. It's in no way akin to the history of natural cross breeding.

  3. Bad actors. Monsanto is the biggest name in GMOs in the US. They have a century long history of putting profit ahead of safety and ethics. Since this is about GMOs and not just Monsanto I'll leave it at that other than to say that this combined with #1 leaves me somewhat uncomfortable.

  4. Correlations. America is fat and rapidly getting fatter. 35% of Americans are obese. 69% are at least overweight. The growth in fat also correlates extremely well with the rise in GMOs. Researchers in Norway have discovered a direct correlation between GMOs and appetite/weight gain in mice. I'm hopeful again that taking corporate interests out of the research process should provide some more clear light on whether there's anything to this.

US expat.

My own stance wasn't clear based on the above. I'm not against GMOs in the least. However, I think that they must be extensively and openly researched before being put onto the market. Right now the process is incredibly opaque and thanks to corruption in America the deputy commission for foods at the FDA, the organization that decides what is safe to eat, is a former Monsanto VP/lobbyist. In the US it seems that corporate and political interests are being put well ahead of safety and research when it comes to GMOs. That's simply dangerous and a recipe for disaster, even if -in this case- the products should turn out to be completely safe.

Ideally, all medical research should be government/charity funded and open in order to decrees corporate influence, or it should be outsourced to an independent, foreign institute. I am not a skeptic on this issue, and I believe it comes from being raised knowing that it is what we do. The U of Minnesota's St Paul campus is almost completely devoted to the studies of agriculture. It is at the edge of the city boundaries, but the suburbs take it from there, so it isn't rural. You can drive past their corn, soybeans, and who knows what else acre. They have another section across the road with trees. They gave us the Honey Crisp and Snowsweet apple strands. The research they do is vast and has created strands that can endure more and can be grown in many environments beyond the original.

With the above said: I don't like the idea that companies are making a fuss over the pollen from GMOs on one field ending up in the farm across the road and suing the farmer who didn't use their seeds. I hate that they have developed them in such a way that they no longer seed correctly naturally, because they are causing everyone to buy their seeds year after year. Which makes me fear for the future. If everyone uses seeds that don't correctly seed, if "shit hits the fan" and we no longer have a way to get those seeds, we will starve to death as a population at our own hands.

I worry about what inserting genes from other organisms does for the quality of the food, or the long-term health of the consumer. However, it undeniably leads to higher food production, and there's been little to no evidence so far that the new genes have a detrimental effect, so I'm fine with GMO foods. I regard pesticides as a greater threat to my health than genetic modification.

A greater problem that I have is the way GMO plants are handled legally. Because companies are allowed to patent their modifications, you have people unable to study them independently, farmers having to pay above and beyond what they'd pay for non-GMO, and so on. Patents have a finite lifetime, but I'd rather not start studying GMO foods 14 years after they're introduced.
